← All statementsWhat are we trying to achieve?
Goal

People in a willing, bounded community can flourish through being-becoming with the world while retaining autonomy and personal boundaries.

Shown in diagrams as: “People flourish through being-becoming with the world, with autonomy and boundaries.”

Where it sits

Contributed by

Ideas from
Margeret Heath
Standing
Proposed; no one has accepted it yet

Where this comes from

  • Margeret Heath, Being-Becoming With the World · Talk 1: Re-membering · spoken script with notes · pp. 27–32, slides 18–20: co-regulation, consent, repair and questions for practice

    Inferred by the AI; this connection is not established by the source.

  • Margeret Heath, Being-Becoming With the World · Talk 1: Re-membering · glossary of 72 terms · pp. 2 and 6: co-regulation and somatic commons

    Inferred by the AI; this connection is not established by the source.

  • Margeret Heath, Being-Becoming With the World · Talk 1: Re-membering · indexed bibliography · p. 13, Part 4: the somatic commons and being-becoming as Heath's syntheses

    Inferred by the AI; this connection is not established by the source.

Source credit does not establish agreement with this wording. Heath commented on an earlier map; this revision awaits her review and endorsement.

Connections

  • Leads into · is needed forParticipation in shared practices is safe, voluntary and open to withdrawal.
  • Leads into · is needed forPeople can notice strain and repair their shared rhythms.
  • Leads into · is needed forTools and environments support purposes that people can question and change.
  • Leads into · is needed forPeople can let encounters with uncertainty reshape their capacities, shared purposes and ways of acting together.

Open questions

  • Choose whose shared conditions and which setting the goal concerns.

    Establish the willing group, situation and scope; no host is yet agreed.

  • Separate evidence for coupling from claims about what constitutes a mind.

    Retain the distinction between empirical coupling, contested constitution and philosophical participation; use the glossary and bibliography to improve source tracing without claiming independent verification. Review the source-first account of process and enmindment; retain the distinction between empirical coupling, contested constitution and philosophical participation.

    Draws on Margeret Heath (document).

History

  • Added in the release of 23 October 2026

  • Reworded in the release of 23 October 2026: Revised to express the fuller argument and bounded scope.

    Earlier wordingPeople can think and act together by tending the bodily, social and material conditions that support them, while retaining agency.

  • Credited in the release of 23 October 2026: Added the supplied glossary and indexed bibliography. Margeret Heath is the sole credited source author across the five original PDFs. Source locators distinguish paraphrase, reconstruction and inference; primary studies have not been independently verified.

  • Reworded in the release of 23 October 2026: Preserved and revised the ten existing review entries and added nine. All reasoning remains proposed; no willing host, trial, assigned action owner, feedback commitment or outcome is established.

  • Reworded in the release of 24 October 2026: Diagram label only: restored being-becoming to the displayed goal; the full statement is unchanged.

    Earlier wordingPeople flourish together while retaining autonomy and personal boundaries.

  • Reworded in the release of 24 October 2026: Added two review entries and extended four. The source account, timing, practical relevance, conflict reconstruction and assessment of capacities and purposes remain open. Novelty can also overwhelm or harm.

Assumptions

  • Candidate assumption to challenge: adequate protection from overwhelm requires externally imposed individual regulation; reliable safeguards might instead be compatible with participant control.

Open questions

  • Test whether adequate safety requires imposed control.

    Challenge the assumption that sufficient safety requires imposed individual control; distinguish reliable safeguards from rigid control.
